topics.name: Bernoulli’s principle
topics.kicker: Faster flow means lower pressure · A key idea behind airplane lift
topics.briefing: Bernoulli’s principle says that when a fluid such as air or water speeds up, its pressure drops. The Swiss scientist Daniel Bernoulli published the idea in his 1738 book _Hydrodynamica_. It helps explain how airplane wings get lift, how perfume sprayers pull up liquid, and why a ping-pong ball can float in the stream from a hair dryer.
topics.answerHtml: Bernoulli’s principle (accept Bernoulli’s equation, Bernoulli’s law, or Bernoulli effect; prompt on Bernoulli; do not accept “Venturi effect”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The 1738 book that introduced this principle, _Hydrodynamica_, also argued that a gas pushes on its container because countless tiny particles keep hitting the walls, an early version of the kinetic theory of gases. That book’s author came from a famous family of mathematicians.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this principle stating that a fluid’s pressure drops as its speed increases.

tossups.p: Leonhard Euler [“OY-ler”] wrote this principle’s equation in its modern form, which applies along a streamline in a steady, incompressible flow with no viscosity. That equation says pressure plus one-half density times speed squared plus density times g times height stays constant.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this rule of fluid dynamics, which says that faster-moving fluids have lower pressure.

tossups.p: This principle’s namesake had a bitter rivalry with his own father, Johann, who wrote a competing book called _Hydraulica_ and dated it earlier than his son’s. The son’s book, _Hydrodynamica_, came out in 1738.
tossups.r: It helps explain airplane lift. For 10 points, name this principle stating that when a fluid flows faster, its pressure falls.

tossups.p: The “equal transit time” fallacy, a popular but wrong explanation of lift that uses this principle, claims that air flowing over the top of an airfoil must meet the air from below at the back edge. In reality, the air over the top arrives first.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this principle of fluids, which helps explain airplane lift by linking faster flow to lower pressure.

tossups.p: In the 1730s, Henri Pitot [“PEE-toh”] invented a tube to measure the speed of river water. Airplanes use such tubes, along with this principle, to find their airspeed by comparing the pressure of air rammed to a stop in the tube with that of the air flowing past.
tossups.r: Perfume sprayers also rely on it. For 10 points, name this principle stating that faster-moving fluids exert less pressure.

tossups.p: A law named for Evangelista Torricelli [“tor-ih-CHEL-ee”] says that water leaks from a hole in a tank at the speed it would reach falling from the water’s surface, and it can be derived from this principle. This principle is really conservation of energy for a moving fluid.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this principle stating that a fluid’s pressure drops when its speed increases.

tossups.p: A Venturi meter uses this principle to find a liquid’s speed by comparing the pressure in a wide part of a pipe with that in a narrow throat, where the liquid moves faster. A carburetor uses the same effect to pull fuel into a stream of air.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this principle, published in 1738, which says that faster fluids have lower pressure.

tossups.p: A 1911 collision between the warship HMS _Hawke_ and the ocean liner _Olympic_, sister ship of the _Titanic_, was blamed on suction explained by this principle. Two ships sailing close together can be pulled toward each other for the same reason.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this principle stating that fast-moving fluids, like the water squeezed between the ships, have lower pressure.

tossups.p: Engineers often write this principle in terms of “head,” saying that pressure head, velocity head, and elevation head add up to a constant total for an ideal fluid. The principle holds exactly only for a fluid with no viscosity that cannot be compressed.
tossups.r: Perfume atomizers use it to draw liquid up a thin tube. For 10 points, name this principle linking faster fluid speed to lower pressure.

tossups.p: A water aspirator in a chemistry lab uses this principle, pulling air out of a flask with a fast jet of water. Race cars carry upside-down wings so that this principle presses them onto the track, a push called downforce.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this principle that explains how airplane wings get lift, because faster-moving air has lower pressure.

tossups.p: This principle is often used with the continuity equation, which says that a fluid in a pipe speeds up wherever the pipe gets narrower, since area times speed stays the same. Blowing between two empty soda cans makes them roll toward each other because of this principle.
tossups.r: It helps explain how airplanes fly. For 10 points, name this principle that says faster-moving fluids exert less pressure.

tossups.p: Blowing hard through an upside-down funnel can hold a ping-pong ball inside instead of pushing it out, and a ping-pong ball can hover in the stream of a hair dryer; both tricks are classroom demonstrations of this principle.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this principle of fluid flow, published by a Swiss scientist in 1738, which helps explain airplane lift.

tossups.p: In this principle’s equation, one-half times density times speed squared is called dynamic pressure; adding it to the static pressure gives the total, or stagnation, pressure. Because of this principle, strong hurricane winds racing over a roof can help lift it off a house.
tossups.r: Wind blowing across a chimney top helps draw smoke up for the same reason. For 10 points, name this principle linking faster fluid flow to lower pressure.

tossups.p: In a Bunsen burner, gas rushing out of a narrow jet pulls air in through holes near the bottom of the barrel, thanks to this principle. Many airbrushes use a fast stream of air to pull paint up from a cup in a similar way.
tossups.r: This principle is named for a Swiss scientist. For 10 points, name this principle stating that faster-moving fluids have lower pressure.

tossups.p: This principle’s namesake, who trained as a doctor, later used mathematics to argue that inoculating people against smallpox would save lives. He described this principle in his 1738 book _Hydrodynamica_, and his father and uncle were also famous mathematicians.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this principle, which says that when a fluid speeds up, its pressure drops.

trap.title: Not Pascal or Venturi
trap.body: Several fluid answer lines sound alike. Pascal’s principle says pressure applied to a trapped fluid spreads equally in all directions, as in hydraulic lifts, and Archimedes’ principle is about buoyancy and floating. The Venturi effect is a special case of this principle in a narrowing pipe, and the Magnus effect is what curves a spinning ball, so real answer lines may refuse those names.
trap.fix: Speed and pressure trading off, wings, sprayers, Pitot tubes, or _Hydrodynamica_ mean this principle. Hydraulic jacks and brakes mean Pascal; floating and displaced water mean Archimedes; a spinning, curving ball means the Magnus effect; and saying just “Bernoulli” earns only a prompt.
trap.line: Real answer line: Bernoulli’s principle (accept Bernoulli’s equation, Bernoulli’s law, or Bernoulli effect; prompt on Bernoulli; do not accept “Venturi effect”)

topics.name: Hall effect
topics.kicker: Sideways voltage from a magnet · Used to sense magnetic fields
topics.briefing: In 1879, a graduate student named Edwin Hall discovered that when an electric current flows through a thin metal strip inside a magnetic field, a small voltage appears across the strip, sideways to the current. The magnetic force pushes the moving charges toward one edge, and that pile-up creates the voltage. Tiny Hall effect sensors detect magnets in phones, cars, and electric motors.
topics.answerHtml: Hall effect (accept specific types such as the quantum Hall effect; prompt on Hall voltage or Hall alone)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1980, Klaus von Klitzing found that in a very thin, very cold layer of electrons, the resistance tied to this effect comes only in values equal to Planck’s constant over the electron’s charge squared, divided by a whole number. He won the 1985 Nobel Prize in Physics.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect in which a magnetic field produces a voltage across a conductor, sideways to the current.

tossups.p: Daniel Tsui and Horst Störmer [“SHTUR-mer”] discovered a “fractional” version of this effect in 1982, which Robert Laughlin explained using strange quasiparticles that carry one-third of an electron’s charge. All three shared the 1998 Nobel Prize in Physics.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, discovered in 1879, in which a sideways voltage appears across a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field.

tossups.p: While a graduate student at Johns Hopkins under Henry Rowland, this effect’s discoverer tested a claim in James Clerk Maxwell’s _Treatise on Electricity and Magnetism_ that a magnet pushes on a wire carrying a current, not on the current itself.
tossups.r: In 1879, he found a tiny voltage across a thin metal strip. For 10 points, name this effect named for that American physicist.

tossups.p: This effect’s namesake coefficient equals one divided by the number of charge carriers per unit volume times their charge, so measuring it tells scientists how many free electrons a metal has. The voltage it produces is larger in a thinner sample.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect in which a magnetic field pushes moving charges to one side of a conductor, creating a voltage.

tossups.p: In some semiconductors, the voltage from this effect points the opposite way from what electrons would produce, showing that the current is carried by positive “holes.” Scientists use this effect to tell n-type semiconductors from p-type ones, and it is much stronger in semiconductors than in metals.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, discovered in 1879, in which a sideways voltage appears across a current-carrying strip in a magnetic field.

tossups.p: SpaceX’s Starlink satellites adjust their orbits with small electric engines named for this effect, which use a magnetic field to trap swirling electrons and an electric field to fire out charged gas. The European probe SMART-1 used one of those engines to reach the Moon in 2004.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect in which a magnetic field creates a sideways voltage in a conductor carrying a current.

tossups.p: Brushless electric motors use tiny sensors based on this effect to track the position of their spinning magnets, and cars use similar sensors to measure wheel speed for anti-lock brakes. Some phones and tablets use them to notice when a magnetic cover is closed.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, the sideways voltage produced across a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field.

tossups.p: National laboratories use a quantized version of this effect as their standard for electrical resistance, and since 2019 the constant h over e squared, about 25,813 ohms, has had an exact value. That constant is named for Klaus von Klitzing.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect in which charges pushed sideways by a magnetic field build up a voltage across a conductor.

tossups.p: The voltage from this effect equals the current times the magnetic field, divided by the product of three things: the density of charge carriers, their charge, and the sample’s thickness. Reversing the magnetic field flips the sign of the voltage this effect produces.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect discovered by an American physicist in 1879, in which a magnetic field makes a sideways voltage across a current.

tossups.p: This effect was discovered in 1879, eighteen years before J. J. Thomson discovered the electron, so its discoverer did not yet know what was actually flowing in a wire. Its voltage is proportional to both the current and the strength of the magnetic field.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect in which a magnetic field pushes moving charges sideways, building up a voltage across a conductor.

tossups.p: When this effect reaches a steady state, the sideways electric force on each moving charge exactly cancels the magnetic part of the Lorentz force, so the charges’ drift speed equals the electric field divided by the magnetic field.
tossups.r: The right-hand rule tells which edge of the conductor the charges pile up on. For 10 points, name this effect, in which a magnetic field creates a sideways voltage.

tossups.p: Teslameters, also called gaussmeters, usually measure the strength of a magnetic field with a small probe based on this effect. Clamp meters that measure direct current in a wire without touching it often rely on the same effect.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, discovered in 1879, in which a voltage appears across a current-carrying strip placed in a magnetic field.

tossups.p: Measurements of this effect, together with resistance, tell chip makers how easily charges move through a semiconductor, a property called mobility. In copper, the direction of the voltage from this effect shows that the charges carrying the current are negative.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, in which a magnetic field produces a voltage across a conductor at right angles to the current.

tossups.p: Some gaming keyboards and joysticks use magnet sensors based on this effect, which have no touching parts to wear out. Many car engines use the same kind of sensor to track the position of the crankshaft.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, the sideways voltage that appears across a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field.

tossups.p: This effect’s American discoverer went on to teach physics at Harvard for many years. He had found this effect while working toward his doctorate at Johns Hopkins University. In this effect, the magnetic field, the current, and the voltage all point at right angles to one another.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this effect, discovered in 1879, that produces a sideways voltage in a conductor sitting in a magnetic field.

trap.title: The effect, not its parts
trap.body: Tossups on this effect are full of its ingredients, so players blurt the wrong piece. The Lorentz force is the magnetic push on moving charges that causes the effect, the “Hall voltage” is only its result, and saying just “Hall” names a person. Other magnetic effects, like the Zeeman effect (split spectral lines) or magnetoresistance (resistance changing in a magnetic field), have their own answer lines.
trap.fix: A current, a magnetic field, and a voltage across the conductor, all at right angles, mean this effect, so say the full name, “Hall effect.” Split spectral lines mean the Zeeman effect, and light knocking electrons out of a metal means the photoelectric effect.
trap.line: Real answer line: Hall effect (accept specific types such as the quantum Hall effect; prompt on Hall voltage or Hall alone)

topics.name: Niels Bohr
topics.kicker: Danish father of the quantum atom · Electrons in fixed orbits
topics.briefing: Niels Bohr was a Danish physicist who, in 1913, pictured the atom as a tiny solar system in which electrons can travel only in certain fixed orbits, jumping between them by giving off or absorbing light. That idea explained the colors of light that glowing hydrogen gives off and helped win him the 1922 Nobel Prize in Physics. His institute in Copenhagen became a world center for the new science of quantum mechanics.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: When this scientist received the Order of the Elephant in 1947, he chose a coat of arms showing the yin-yang symbol and the Latin motto “Contraria sunt complementa,” or “opposites are complementary.” That motto reflected his principle of complementarity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Danish physicist whose 1913 model of the atom placed electrons in fixed orbits.

tossups.p: This scientist’s theory of the periodic table predicted that element 72 would resemble zirconium rather than the rare earths, and in 1923 two researchers at his institute found it and named it hafnium, after the Latin name for his home city.
tossups.r: Element 107 is also named for him. For 10 points, name this Danish physicist who proposed a model of the hydrogen atom in 1913.

tossups.p: In 1940, as German troops occupied Copenhagen, George de Hevesy [“HEV-eh-shee”] dissolved the gold Nobel Prize medals of Max von Laue and James Franck in aqua regia at this scientist’s institute to hide them from the Nazis. The gold was later recovered and the medals were recast.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Danish physicist who won the 1922 Nobel Prize for his model of the atom.

tossups.p: In 1943, this scientist escaped from occupied Denmark to Sweden on a fishing boat, then flew to Britain in the bomb bay of a Mosquito airplane and passed out from lack of oxygen. He later advised the Manhattan Project under the false name “Nicholas Baker.”
tossups.r: His son Aage later won a Nobel Prize too. For 10 points, name this Danish physicist who modeled the atom with electrons in fixed orbits.

tossups.p: In 1939, this scientist and John Wheeler explained nuclear fission with a liquid-drop model of the nucleus, and he realized that the rare isotope uranium-235 is the one that splits when hit by slow neutrons. Earlier that year, he had carried news of fission’s discovery to the United States.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Danish physicist whose 1913 atomic model put electrons in fixed energy levels.

tossups.p: At a 1927 conference in Como, Italy, this scientist introduced complementarity, the idea that light and electrons show wave or particle behavior depending on the experiment, but never both at once. He and Werner Heisenberg developed the Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Danish physicist who won the 1922 Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on atomic structure.

tossups.p: This scientist’s correspondence principle says that quantum physics must give the same answers as classical physics for very large quantum numbers, such as electrons in huge orbits. In his model, an electron’s angular momentum must be a whole-number multiple of Planck’s constant divided by two pi.
tossups.r: That model explained the lines in hydrogen’s spectrum. For 10 points, name this Danish physicist who proposed it in 1913.

tossups.p: At the 1930 Solvay Conference, this scientist answered Albert Einstein’s “photon box” challenge to quantum mechanics by using Einstein’s own general relativity. This scientist also replied to a famous 1935 paper by Einstein, Podolsky, and Rosen.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Danish physicist whose 1913 model of the atom had electrons jumping between fixed orbits.

tossups.p: After working with Ernest Rutherford in Manchester, this scientist published a three-part paper in 1913, often called his “trilogy,” in the journal _Philosophical Magazine_. That work explained the Balmer series of visible lines in hydrogen’s spectrum and the value of the Rydberg constant.
tossups.r: In his model, electrons give off light when they jump down between fixed orbits. For 10 points, name this Danish physicist.

tossups.p: Michael Frayn’s 1998 play _Copenhagen_ imagines what this scientist and his former assistant Werner Heisenberg said during a mysterious 1941 meeting in German-occupied Denmark. The play’s third character is this scientist’s wife, Margrethe.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Danish physicist who won the 1922 Nobel Prize for his work on the structure of atoms.

tossups.p: This scientist’s son Aage won the 1975 Nobel Prize in Physics for work on the structure of atomic nuclei, and his father, Christian, found that carbon dioxide helps blood release oxygen. His brother Harald was a mathematician who won an Olympic silver medal in soccer.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Danish physicist whose model of the atom had electrons in fixed orbits.

tossups.p: The radius of the smallest electron orbit in this scientist’s model of hydrogen, about 0.053 nanometers, is named for him. Arnold Sommerfeld later improved this scientist’s model by allowing electrons to follow elliptical orbits.
tossups.r: His model could not explain atoms with more than one electron, such as helium. For 10 points, name this Danish physicist who proposed that model in 1913.

tossups.p: In 1944, this scientist urged Winston Churchill and Franklin Roosevelt to tell the Soviet Union about the atomic bomb project to avoid an arms race, and in 1950 he wrote an open letter to the United Nations calling for an “open world.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Danish physicist whose model of the atom had electrons jumping between fixed orbits.

tossups.p: In 1921, this scientist opened an institute for theoretical physics at the University of Copenhagen, where young physicists like Werner Heisenberg and Wolfgang Pauli came to work. The institute was later renamed for him.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Danish physicist whose 1913 model of the hydrogen atom placed electrons in fixed orbits.

tossups.p: This scientist’s Nobel Prize in Physics was announced at the same time as Albert Einstein’s delayed prize for 1921. This scientist had earlier worked with J. J. Thomson at Cambridge before moving to Manchester to work with Ernest Rutherford.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this Danish physicist whose atomic model placed electrons in fixed, numbered energy levels.

trap.title: Not Rutherford or Heisenberg
trap.body: Several founders of atomic physics show up in the same tossups. Ernest Rutherford discovered the nucleus with his gold foil experiment, and this man then put the electrons into fixed orbits around it; Werner Heisenberg, his younger colleague, created matrix mechanics and the uncertainty principle. The family is a trap too: his son Aage won a Nobel Prize in 1975, and his father Christian’s name is on the Bohr effect in blood.
trap.fix: Fixed orbits, energy levels, hydrogen’s spectrum, complementarity, Copenhagen, or element 107 mean this man. The gold foil experiment and the nucleus mean Rutherford; matrix mechanics and uncertainty mean Heisenberg; and a 1975 Nobel for work on atomic nuclei means his son Aage, so give the full name if you can.
trap.line: Real answer line: Niels Bohr (accept Bohr; do not accept “Aage Bohr”)

topics.name: Precession
topics.kicker: A spinning axis that sweeps out a cone · Why the North Star changes
topics.dates: Discovered for Earth by Hipparchus, second century BCE
topics.briefing: Set a top spinning at a tilt and its axis doesn’t just fall over: it slowly sweeps around in a circle. That motion is precession, and Earth does it too. Tugged by the Sun and Moon, Earth’s axis traces a full circle about every 26,000 years, so the North Star changes: Thuban was the pole star when the pyramids were built, and Vega will be close to the pole in about 12,000 years.
topics.answerHtml: precession (accept word forms like precessing; prompt on wobble; do not accept “nutation”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Of the three Euler [“OY-ler”] angles that describe how a rigid body is turned in space, one is named for spin, one for a nodding motion called nutation, and one for this motion. During this motion, a torque changes the direction of a spinning object’s angular momentum but not its size.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this motion in which a spinning object’s axis slowly sweeps out a cone.

tossups.p: In the second century BCE, the Greek astronomer Hipparchus [“hih-PAR-kus”] discovered this motion of Earth by noticing that the bright star Spica sat in a different spot than older records showed. This motion slides the equinox points westward around the sky by about one degree every 72 years.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this slow wobble of Earth’s axis, which completes a full circle about every 26,000 years.

tossups.p: Because of this motion, the star Thuban [“THOO-bahn”] in the constellation Draco was the pole star when the Egyptian pyramids were built. The pull of the Sun’s and Moon’s gravity on Earth’s bulging equator causes this motion.
tossups.r: In about 12,000 years, it will make Vega the North Star. For 10 points, name this slow wobble of Earth’s axis.

tossups.p: In 1859, Urbain Le Verrier [“ur-BAN luh vair-YAY”] found that Newton’s laws could not fully explain this motion of Mercury’s orbit, so he suggested an unseen planet, later named Vulcan. In 1915, Albert Einstein used general relativity to explain the extra 43 arcseconds per century of this motion.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this motion, which also makes a tilted spinning top’s axis slowly circle around.

tossups.p: NASA’s Gravity Probe B carried four gyroscopes with rotors made of nearly perfect balls of fused quartz to measure tiny amounts of this motion predicted by general relativity. A spinning bicycle wheel hung from a rope by one end of its axle shows this motion.
tossups.r: Its axle swings slowly around the rope instead of falling. For 10 points, name this motion of a spinning object’s axis.

tossups.p: In an MRI scanner, the magnetic moments of protons in the body’s water molecules undergo this motion around a strong magnetic field at a rate called the Larmor [“LAR-mor”] frequency. That rate rises as the magnetic field gets stronger.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this motion, also seen when the axis of a tilted spinning top slowly circles around.

tossups.p: This motion makes the tropical year, measured from one March equinox to the next, about 20 minutes shorter than the sidereal year, measured against the stars. Along with changes in Earth’s tilt and the shape of its orbit, it is one of the three Milankovitch [“mih-LAHN-koh-vitch”] cycles that help pace the ice ages.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this slow wobble that makes Earth’s axis trace a circle about every 26,000 years.

tossups.p: In his _Principia_, Isaac Newton explained this motion of Earth as the result of the Sun’s and Moon’s gravity tugging on Earth’s equatorial bulge. That tug is a torque, and it changes the direction Earth’s axis points without changing how much the axis is tilted.
tossups.r: It slowly changes which star is the North Star. For 10 points, name this slow wobble of Earth’s spin axis.

tossups.p: Because of this motion, the point where the Sun crosses the celestial equator in March, still called the First Point of Aries, has drifted into the constellation Pisces. For the same reason, the Sun no longer sits in Cancer at the June solstice, though the Tropic of Cancer kept its name.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this slow motion of Earth’s axis, which takes about 26,000 years to complete.

tossups.p: James Bradley discovered that Earth’s axis also nods slightly back and forth in an 18.6-year cycle, a smaller motion called nutation that rides on top of this larger motion. Both motions are caused mainly by the gravity of the Moon and the Sun.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this slow wobble that makes Earth’s axis trace out a cone, taking about 26,000 years for each circle.

tossups.p: Spinning a toy gyroscope faster makes this motion slower, because the rate of this motion equals the torque from gravity divided by the gyroscope’s angular momentum. Pushing down on one end of a spinning gyroscope’s axle makes the axle move sideways, at right angles to the push.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this motion in which a tilted spinning top’s axis slowly circles around instead of falling over.

tossups.p: One full cycle of this motion of Earth is sometimes called a “Great Year” or a “Platonic year.” If Earth were a perfect sphere, the Sun and Moon could not twist it, and Earth would not undergo this motion.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this slow wobble of Earth’s axis, which takes about 26,000 years to complete one circle.

tossups.p: Earth’s equatorial bulge makes the planes of satellite orbits slowly turn in a form of this motion, which sun-synchronous satellites use so that they always cross the equator at the same local time of day. The tilted plane of the Moon’s orbit also turns this way, mainly because of the Sun’s pull, once every 18.6 years.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this motion, which also makes Earth’s spin axis trace a slow circle in the sky.

tossups.p: The swing of a Foucault [“foo-KOH”] pendulum slowly turns in a form of this motion, making a full circle in about a day at the North Pole but not turning at all at the equator. In 1852, Léon Foucault named the gyroscope, which he used to show that Earth rotates.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this motion in which a spinning top’s tilted axis slowly sweeps around in a cone.

tossups.p: Star catalogs give positions for a fixed date, such as the start of the year 2000, because this motion slowly shifts the sky coordinates of every star. In astrology, the “Age of Aquarius” refers to the time when this motion carries the March equinox point into Aquarius.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this slow wobble of Earth’s axis, which takes about 26,000 years per cycle.

trap.title: Precession or nutation?
trap.body: Precession is the big, slow circling of a spinning axis; nutation is the smaller nodding wobble that rides on top of it, and one Euler angle is named for each, so tossups mention both. Earth questions add more traps: rotation is the daily spin, revolution is the yearly orbit, and the slow change in how far Earth tilts (obliquity) is a separate Milankovitch cycle.
trap.fix: A cone traced by a spinning axis, a 26,000-year cycle, Hipparchus, drifting equinoxes, or a changing North Star means precession. A small nod with an 18.6-year period means nutation. If the question asks for the quantity the torque changes, say angular momentum.
trap.line: Real answer line: precession (accept word forms like precessing; prompt on wobble; do not accept “nutation”)

topics.name: Brownian motion
topics.kicker: Random jiggling of tiny specks in a fluid · Proof that molecules exist
topics.dates: Observed by Robert Brown, 1827; explained by Einstein, 1905
topics.briefing: In 1827, botanist Robert Brown peered through his microscope at tiny particles from pollen grains floating in water and saw them jiggling nonstop, as if alive. That random dance, Brownian motion, happens because invisible water molecules keep slamming into the particles from every side. In 1905 Albert Einstein worked out the math, and Jean Perrin’s experiments that followed helped convince doubters that atoms and molecules are real.
topics.answerHtml: Brownian motion (accept Brownian movement, pedesis, or Wiener process; prompt on random walk; do not accept “diffusion”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In his 1900 thesis, Louis Bachelier [“bah-shel-YAY”] used a mathematical version of this phenomenon to model the ups and downs of prices on the Paris stock exchange. In that model, prices take a random walk, moving up or down by chance at each step.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this random jiggling of tiny particles suspended in a fluid, named for a Scottish botanist.

tossups.p: In _On the Nature of Things_, the Roman poet Lucretius [“loo-KREE-shus”] described dust specks dancing in a sunbeam as evidence that unseen atoms were pushing them, an early description often linked to this phenomenon. Jean Perrin’s measurements of this phenomenon later helped convince doubters that atoms really exist.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this random jiggling of particles in a fluid, which Robert Brown saw under a microscope in 1827.

tossups.p: In 1785, the Dutch scientist Jan Ingenhousz [“ING-en-howss”], better known for showing that plants need light to make oxygen, described coal dust jittering on the surface of alcohol, an early sighting of this phenomenon. Smaller particles show more of this motion than larger ones.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this random movement of particles suspended in a fluid, named for the botanist Robert Brown.

tossups.p: Paul Langevin [“lahn-zhuh-VAN”] described this phenomenon in 1908 with an equation that combines a drag force that slows a particle with a rapidly changing random force. This phenomenon grows more vigorous as the surrounding fluid gets warmer.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this random jiggling of particles from pollen grains and other specks in water, which Robert Brown studied in 1827.

tossups.p: Jean Perrin [“zhahn peh-RAN”] tracked tiny grains of a yellow resin called gamboge [“gam-BOHJ”] to test a theory of this phenomenon, work that earned him the 1926 Nobel Prize in Physics. He used his results to calculate Avogadro’s number.
tossups.r: Albert Einstein had explained this phenomenon in 1905. For 10 points, name this random jiggling of small particles in a fluid.

tossups.p: A particle undergoing this phenomenon wanders a typical distance from its starting point that grows only with the square root of time, so drifting twice as far takes four times as long. Measuring this phenomenon gave scientists a way to find Avogadro’s number.
tossups.r: Albert Einstein explained it in 1905. For 10 points, name this random jiggling of tiny particles in a fluid, named for Robert Brown.

tossups.p: In a common school experiment, a microscope aimed into a small glass cell full of smoke shows bright specks wobbling unpredictably because of this phenomenon. The specks keep moving this way for as long as anyone watches; the motion never runs down.
tossups.r: It happens because invisible air molecules keep crashing into the specks. For 10 points, name this random jiggling named for botanist Robert Brown.

tossups.p: This phenomenon’s namesake sailed to Australia with Matthew Flinders as the naturalist aboard HMS _Investigator_ and later named the cell nucleus. He showed that this phenomenon was not a sign of life by seeing it in specks of ground glass and rock.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this random jiggling of tiny particles in water, studied by a Scottish botanist in 1827.

tossups.p: This phenomenon is named for a botanist who saw it while studying pollen from the wildflower _Clarkia pulchella_ [“KLAR-kee-uh pul-KEL-uh”], and who at first wondered if the moving particles were alive. Those particles came from inside the pollen grains.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this random jiggling of tiny particles in a fluid, named for Robert Brown.

tossups.p: Another name for this phenomenon comes from a Greek word meaning “leaping.” The Stokes–Einstein equation says that this phenomenon spreads particles faster at higher temperatures and more slowly in thicker, more viscous liquids.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this random zigzag motion of small particles in a fluid, named for Robert Brown.

tossups.p: Marian Smoluchowski [“smoh-loo-KOF-skee”] explained this phenomenon in 1906, separately from a more famous physicist, with an equation linking how fast the particles spread to their mobility and the temperature. Whole pollen grains are too big to show this phenomenon clearly, but tiny particles released from inside them do.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this random jiggling of tiny particles in a fluid, which Robert Brown studied in 1827.

tossups.p: Norbert Wiener [“WEE-ner”] gave the first rigorous mathematical description of this phenomenon, so mathematicians name their model of it for him. In that model, a particle’s position after a set time follows a bell-shaped normal distribution.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this random jiggling of tiny particles suspended in a fluid, named for a Scottish botanist.

tossups.p: A particle undergoing this phenomenon is just as likely to move one way as any other, yet over time it wanders farther and farther from where it started. This phenomenon is the microscopic process behind diffusion, the spreading of particles from crowded areas to less crowded ones.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this random jiggling of tiny particles in a fluid, caused by collisions with molecules.

tossups.p: Richard Feynman’s ratchet-and-pawl thought experiment showed that a tiny one-way gear cannot turn this phenomenon into useful work when everything is at the same temperature. Particles undergoing this phenomenon wander farther in thin liquids like water than in thick ones like honey.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this random jiggling of small particles in a fluid, which Albert Einstein explained in 1905.

tossups.p: Under a microscope, droplets of fat in diluted milk jitter back and forth because of this phenomenon, which helps keep the tiny particles in many colloids from settling out. Larger particles show less of it, because the random pushes they get from all sides nearly cancel out.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this random jiggling of small particles in a fluid, named for the Scottish botanist Robert Brown.

trap.title: The motion, not diffusion
trap.body: This jiggling of single particles and diffusion, the overall spreading of a substance, are separate answer lines, and diffusion tossups even mention this motion. Robert Brown is the man, not the answer, and the pollen grains themselves are a separate biology answer line. Saying only “random walk” earns a prompt.
trap.fix: One speck zigzagging under a microscope, Robert Brown in 1827, Einstein’s 1905 paper, Perrin, gamboge, Langevin, or Bachelier means Brownian motion. A substance spreading from high to low concentration, or Fick’s laws, means diffusion. Finish the answer with “motion.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Brownian motion (accept Brownian movement, pedesis, or Wiener process; prompt on random walk; do not accept “diffusion”)

topics.name: Absolute zero
topics.kicker: The coldest possible temperature · Zero on the Kelvin scale
topics.dates: Estimated by Amontons, c. 1702; Kelvin’s absolute scale proposed, 1848
topics.briefing: Absolute zero is the coldest anything can ever get: 0 kelvins, or about −273 °C (−459.67 °F). There, particles have the least energy they possibly can, though quantum physics says they never sit perfectly still. The third law of thermodynamics says no one can ever quite reach it, but scientists using lasers and magnets have chilled atoms to within a billionth of a degree, close enough to make strange new states of matter.
topics.answerHtml: absolute zero (accept 0 kelvins or 0 K; accept −273.15 °C or −459.67 °F; prompt on zero, or on −273 or −459.67 with no unit; do not accept “0 degrees Celsius”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Around 1702, Guillaume Amontons [“ah-mohn-TOHN”] reasoned that the pressure of air would drop to nothing if the air were cooled enough, an early estimate of this temperature. Extending graphs of a gas’s volume against its temperature down to zero volume, following Charles’s law, also points to this temperature.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this lowest possible temperature, the zero point of the Kelvin scale.

tossups.p: Walther Nernst’s heat theorem grew into a law stating that no process can reach this temperature in a finite number of steps. That same law says that the entropy of a perfect crystal is zero at this temperature.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this coldest possible temperature, about 273 degrees below zero on the Celsius scale.

tossups.p: In 1908, Heike Kamerlingh Onnes [“HAY-kuh KAH-mer-ling ON-us”] became the first person to liquefy helium, and three years later he used that liquid to cool mercury to about 4 kelvins above this temperature, discovering superconductivity. He won the 1913 Nobel Prize in Physics for his work near this temperature.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this lowest possible temperature, the zero point of the Kelvin scale.

tossups.p: Steven Chu’s “optical molasses” used crossed laser beams to slow atoms as if they were moving through syrup, chilling them close to this temperature. Chu shared the 1997 Nobel Prize in Physics with Claude Cohen-Tannoudji [“koh-EN tah-noo-JEE”] and William Phillips for such laser cooling.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this coldest possible temperature, 0 on the Kelvin scale.

tossups.p: In 1995, Eric Cornell and Carl Wieman cooled rubidium atoms to less than a millionth of a degree above this temperature, making the first Bose–Einstein condensate. Wolfgang Ketterle shared the 2001 Nobel Prize in Physics with them for such work.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this coldest possible temperature, about 273 degrees below zero on the Celsius scale.

tossups.p: Because of zero-point energy, helium would stay liquid even at this temperature unless it were squeezed to about 25 times normal air pressure. Quantum physics says particles keep that small, unavoidable energy even here, so their motion never stops completely.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this lowest possible temperature, the zero point of the Kelvin scale.

tossups.p: In a metal at this temperature, electrons fill every energy level up to one named for Enrico Fermi, because the Pauli exclusion principle keeps them from all crowding into the lowest level. Even so, those electrons keep moving quickly at this temperature.
tossups.r: On the Fahrenheit scale, it is exactly −459.67 degrees. For 10 points, name this lowest possible temperature.

tossups.p: In 1848, William Thomson proposed a temperature scale that does not depend on any particular substance; the modern scale named for him starts at this temperature. The Rankine [“RANG-kin”] scale also starts at this temperature but uses degrees the same size as Fahrenheit degrees.
tossups.r: Thomson was later called Lord Kelvin. For 10 points, name this lowest possible temperature.

tossups.p: The Boomerang Nebula, at about 1 kelvin, is the coldest known natural place in the universe, even colder than the 2.7-kelvin glow of the cosmic microwave background left over from the Big Bang. Both are only slightly warmer than this temperature.
tossups.r: The third law of thermodynamics says it can never actually be reached. For 10 points, name this coldest possible temperature.

tossups.p: In 1933, William Giauque [“jee-OHK”] used adiabatic demagnetization, which cools a magnetic salt by slowly switching off a strong magnet, to come within a fraction of a degree of this temperature. Giauque won the 1949 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for studying substances near this temperature.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this lowest possible temperature, the zero point of the Kelvin scale.

tossups.p: Dilution refrigerators come within a few thousandths of a degree of this temperature by mixing two isotopes of helium, helium-3 and helium-4. Quantum computers built from superconducting circuits are often kept cold inside such refrigerators.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this coldest possible temperature, about 273 degrees below zero on the Celsius scale.

tossups.p: In 1937, Pyotr Kapitsa [“kuh-PEET-suh”] helped discover that liquid helium cooled below about 2.2 kelvins flows with no viscosity at all, becoming a superfluid. Kapitsa won the 1978 Nobel Prize in Physics for his research on matter at temperatures close to this one.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this lowest possible temperature, which the Kelvin scale calls zero.

tossups.p: NASA’s Cold Atom Laboratory, aboard the International Space Station, chills clouds of atoms to within a tiny fraction of a degree of this temperature, and floating in orbit lets scientists study them longer than on Earth. An ideal gas held at constant volume would exert no pressure at this temperature.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this coldest possible temperature, 0 on the Kelvin scale, which can never quite be reached.

tossups.p: A perfect Carnot [“kar-NOH”] heat engine could turn all of its heat into work only if its cold side were at this temperature, which is impossible. In the classical picture of gases, molecules would have no kinetic energy at all at this temperature.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this lowest possible temperature, the zero point of the Kelvin scale.

tossups.p: The superconducting magnets of the Large Hadron Collider are cooled with superfluid helium to 1.9 kelvins, less than two degrees above this temperature. Hospital MRI machines also use magnets chilled by liquid helium to about 4 kelvins above it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this coldest possible temperature, about 460 degrees below zero on the Fahrenheit scale.

trap.title: Kelvin zero, not Celsius
trap.body: Zero degrees Celsius is just the freezing point of water, and 0 °F is an ordinary cold winter day; only zero on the Kelvin (or Rankine) scale is absolute zero. Players also blurt “temperature,” “third law of thermodynamics,” or “Bose–Einstein condensate,” which are separate answer lines whose tossups mention this one.
trap.fix: If the question asks for “this temperature,” the coldest possible, where the Kelvin scale starts, say absolute zero (or 0 K, about −273 °C). If it asks for “this law,” the answer is the third law of thermodynamics; if it asks for “this state of matter,” it is a Bose–Einstein condensate.
trap.line: Real answer line: absolute zero (accept 0 kelvins or 0 K; accept −273.15 °C or −459.67 °F; prompt on zero, or on −273 or −459.67 with no unit; do not accept “0 degrees Celsius”)

topics.name: Michelson–Morley experiment
topics.kicker: The 1887 search for the aether · Physics’ most famous “failed” experiment
topics.briefing: In 1887, Albert Michelson and Edward Morley set out in Cleveland, Ohio, to measure Earth rushing through the “aether,” an invisible substance that light waves were supposed to travel through. Their instrument, floating on a pool of mercury, split a light beam in two and compared the halves, but it found no sign of the aether at all. That famous “null result” is explained by Einstein’s special relativity, which needs no aether.
topics.answerHtml: Michelson–Morley experiment (prompt on partial answers like Michelson experiment; prompt on Michelson interferometer)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Six years before this experiment, one of its leaders tried a simpler version in Germany, moving it to Potsdam because street traffic in Berlin shook his instrument too much. The two scientists behind this experiment reported their results in an 1887 paper titled “On the Relative Motion of the Earth and the Luminiferous Ether.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this experiment that failed to detect the aether, carried out in Cleveland, Ohio.

tossups.p: Mirrors in this experiment bounced light back and forth to make each of its two paths about 11 meters long. To keep vibrations from spoiling the measurements, the instrument sat on a heavy stone slab floating on a pool of mercury, so it could be turned smoothly.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1887 experiment that looked for the luminiferous aether but found no sign of it.

tossups.p: To explain this experiment’s result, George FitzGerald and Hendrik Lorentz [“LOR-ents”] separately proposed that objects shrink slightly in the direction they move. Albert Einstein’s special relativity later made the aether that this experiment was looking for unnecessary.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1887 experiment by two American scientists, which found no evidence of an aether wind.

tossups.p: The scientists behind this experiment expected the interference fringes they watched to shift by about four-tenths of a fringe as their instrument turned, but they saw only a tiny fraction of that. This experiment’s “null result” has been called the most famous failed experiment in physics.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1887 experiment that tried to detect Earth’s motion through the aether.

tossups.p: Because Earth orbits the Sun at about 30 kilometers per second, the scientists behind this experiment expected an “aether wind” to make light travel at slightly different speeds in different directions. They turned their instrument and repeated the measurements at different times of day.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this experiment in Cleveland, Ohio, that found no sign of the luminiferous aether.

tossups.p: One leader of this experiment was a chemist known for carefully measuring the atomic weight of oxygen. The other became, in 1907, the first American to win a Nobel Prize in a science, honored for his precise optical instruments rather than for this experiment itself.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1887 experiment that found no evidence of the luminiferous aether.

tossups.p: In the 1920s, Dayton Miller claimed to have found a small aether wind while repeating this experiment on Mount Wilson in California, but other scientists could not confirm his results. This experiment used an interferometer, which splits a light beam in two and then recombines it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1887 experiment whose “null result” showed no sign of the aether.

tossups.p: The Kennedy–Thorndike experiment of 1932 changed this experiment’s design by making the two arms of its instrument different lengths. Like that later test, this experiment found no sign that the speed of light depends on how the instrument moves.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1887 experiment that tried to detect the luminiferous aether.

tossups.p: The LIGO observatories, which first detected gravitational waves in 2015, are giant versions of the kind of instrument used in this experiment, with arms 4 kilometers long. That kind of instrument is named for one of this experiment’s two leaders.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1887 experiment that found no sign of an aether wind.

tossups.p: In 1886, the two scientists behind this experiment repeated Hippolyte Fizeau’s [“fee-ZOHZ”] test of how fast light travels through flowing water, confirming a formula by Augustin-Jean Fresnel [“freh-NEL”]. A year later, they began this more famous experiment in Cleveland, Ohio.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this experiment that failed to detect Earth’s motion through the luminiferous aether.

tossups.p: In this experiment, a half-silvered mirror split a beam of light into two beams that traveled at right angles to each other, bounced off mirrors, and then recombined to make light and dark bands called interference fringes. Those fringes barely shifted when the instrument was turned.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1887 experiment whose “null result” found no evidence of the aether.

tossups.p: The supposed substance that this experiment tried to detect was called “luminiferous,” meaning “light-bearing,” because scientists thought light waves needed it to travel, the way sound needs air. This experiment found no sign of that substance.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1887 experiment that failed to detect the aether, a famous “null result.”

tossups.p: The two scientists who carried out this experiment worked at neighboring schools in Cleveland, Ohio, which later merged to form Case Western Reserve University. They rotated their instrument to look for changes in how fast light moved along its two arms.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1887 experiment that found no sign of the luminiferous aether.

tossups.p: James Bradley’s discovery of the aberration of starlight in the 1720s suggested that Earth plows through a motionless aether, but this experiment found no sign of the “aether wind” that such motion should cause. This experiment checked whether light moved at the same speed along two paths at right angles.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1887 experiment performed in Cleveland, Ohio, which produced a famous “null result.”

tossups.p: Albert Einstein’s 1905 rule that light travels at the same speed for every observer fits the result of this experiment, though historians debate how much this experiment influenced him. Its result surprised physicists, who expected light’s speed to depend on the direction Earth was moving.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this 1887 experiment that failed to find the luminiferous aether.

Found no sign of an aether wind: a famous “null result”
Carried out in 1887 in Cleveland, Ohio, by two American scientists

Its result fits Albert Einstein’s special relativity, which does away with the aether
Light’s speed came out the same along both paths, no matter which way the instrument pointed

A half-silvered mirror split the beam; the two beams traveled at right angles and recombined into interference fringes

trap.title: The test, not the aether
trap.body: Tossups on this experiment are full of the aether, special relativity, and length contraction, but each of those is its own answer line; the question wants the 1887 test itself. It is also easy to mix up with the Millikan oil drop experiment, another famous American physics experiment whose name starts with “Mi-.” Naming only one scientist, or only the interferometer, earns just a prompt.
trap.fix: Light beams, mirrors, interference fringes, an aether wind, a stone slab floating on mercury, or a “null result” means Michelson–Morley. Charged oil drops and the electron’s charge mean Millikan. Say both names: “Michelson–Morley experiment.”
trap.line: Real answer line: Michelson–Morley experiment (prompt on partial answers like Michelson experiment; prompt on Michelson interferometer)

topics.name: Higgs boson
topics.kicker: The particle of the mass-giving Higgs field · Found at CERN in 2012
topics.briefing: The Higgs boson is a short-lived particle whose discovery at CERN’s Large Hadron Collider was announced on July 4, 2012, almost 50 years after Peter Higgs and others predicted it. It belongs to the Higgs field, an invisible field filling all of space that gives elementary particles such as electrons and quarks their mass. Without that field, electrons would have no mass, and atoms as we know them could not exist.
topics.answerHtml: Higgs boson (accept Higgs particle or God particle; prompt on boson; do not accept “Higgs field” or “Higgs mechanism”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This particle is made most often when two gluons fuse, and it was first spotted through its decays into two photons or into four leptons. It breaks apart far less than a trillionth of a second after it forms.
tossups.r: Its discovery at CERN was announced in 2012. For 10 points, name this particle linked to a field that gives other particles mass.

tossups.p: Finding this particle was a main goal of the Superconducting Super Collider, a giant accelerator in Texas that Congress canceled in 1993. Fermilab’s Tevatron searched for this particle until the Tevatron shut down in 2011.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this particle discovered at the Large Hadron Collider in 2012, which is connected to how other particles get mass.

tossups.p: After a journal turned down one of his 1964 papers, this particle’s namesake added a paragraph pointing out that his theory predicted a new particle. François Englert and Robert Brout independently proposed the same mass-giving mechanism that year.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this particle discovered at CERN in 2012 and named for a British physicist.

tossups.p: The energy of the field linked to this particle is often drawn as a “Mexican hat” or “wine bottle” shape with its lowest point off-center, so the field has a nonzero value even in completely empty space. That off-center low point “breaks” a symmetry of the laws of physics.
tossups.r: Particles that interact with that field gain mass. For 10 points, name this particle discovered in 2012.

tossups.p: In papers published in 2012, the ATLAS and CMS teams each reached the “five sigma” level of confidence needed to claim the discovery of this particle, which has a mass of about 125 billion electron volts.
tossups.r: Its discovery was announced on July 4, 2012. For 10 points, name this particle found at the Large Hadron Collider, linked to the field that gives particles mass.

tossups.p: This particle got a famous nickname from the title of Leon Lederman’s 1993 book about it, a nickname that the physicist this particle is named for reportedly disliked. Lederman had shared a Nobel Prize for discovering the muon neutrino.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this particle discovered at CERN in 2012, which is linked to a field that gives other particles mass.

tossups.p: A famous 1993 explanation of this particle, written for a British science minister’s contest, compared its field to guests at a party who crowd around a celebrity crossing the room, slowing that person down the way the field gives particles mass. In that comparison, this particle is like a rumor that makes the guests bunch together.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this particle whose discovery was announced at CERN in 2012, linked to a field that gives particles mass.

tossups.p: The top quark, the heaviest known elementary particle, interacts more strongly with this particle’s field than any other particle does. This particle has about 133 times the mass of a proton.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this particle, discovered at the Large Hadron Collider in 2012, that is tied to how elementary particles get mass.

tossups.p: This particle is the only known elementary particle with a spin of zero, which makes it the only known fundamental “scalar” particle. It has no electric charge and breaks apart almost instantly after it forms.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this particle discovered at CERN in 2012 and nicknamed for the title of a book by Leon Lederman.

tossups.p: Steven Weinberg and Abdus Salam built the mass-giving idea behind this particle into Sheldon Glashow’s theory uniting electromagnetism and the weak force. Through electroweak symmetry breaking, the field linked to this particle gives mass to the W and Z bosons, which carry the weak force, while leaving the photon massless.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this particle found at the Large Hadron Collider, linked to a field that gives elementary particles mass.

tossups.p: Only about one percent of a proton’s mass comes from the field linked to this particle, since most of it comes from the energy of the strong force that binds the proton’s quarks together.
tossups.r: That field does give electrons their mass. For 10 points, name this particle discovered at CERN in 2012.

tossups.p: This particle most often decays into a pair of bottom quarks, though it was first found through rarer decays. It breaks apart in less than a billionth of a trillionth of a second, so detectors see only the particles it leaves behind.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this particle found at the Large Hadron Collider in 2012, linked to a field that gives particles mass.

tossups.p: Gerald Guralnik, Carl Hagen, and Tom Kibble wrote one of three 1964 papers describing how a field could give particles mass, an idea later tied to this particle. The author of a different one of those papers is this particle’s namesake.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this particle whose 2012 discovery at CERN confirmed that idea.

tossups.p: This particle belongs to a class named for Satyendra Nath Bose, made of particles with whole-number spin, but unlike photons and gluons, it is not a carrier of one of the four fundamental forces. It has no electric charge.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this particle discovered at CERN in 2012 and named for a British physicist.

tossups.p: The 2013 Nobel Prize in Physics went to François Englert and a British physicist for predicting the mechanism behind this particle; Englert’s partner, Robert Brout, had died in 2011. That prize came one year after this particle’s discovery was announced.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this particle found at the Large Hadron Collider, which is linked to a field that gives other particles mass.

trap.body: This particle, the field it belongs to, the mass-giving “mechanism,” and the physicist Peter Higgs are all different answers, and real answer lines can refuse “Higgs field” on a particle question. Weak-force tossups also mention the Higgs mechanism, since it gives the W and Z bosons their mass, so do not buzz with this particle there.
trap.fix: If the question asks for “this particle,” found at the Large Hadron Collider in 2012, say “Higgs boson.” If it asks for “this field” or “this mechanism,” name the field or the mechanism; if it asks for “this physicist,” say Peter Higgs. Just “boson” earns only a prompt.

topics.name: Neutrons
topics.kicker: The neutral particle in the nucleus · Key to isotopes and chain reactions
topics.briefing: Neutrons are the uncharged particles packed into the nucleus of almost every atom alongside protons, and each one is just slightly heavier than a proton. James Chadwick discovered them in 1932. Changing the number of neutrons makes a different isotope of the same element, and neutrons trigger nuclear chain reactions: when one splits a uranium-235 nucleus, two or three more fly out to split others.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1930, Walther Bothe [“BOH-tuh”] and Herbert Becker found that beryllium struck by alpha particles gave off a penetrating radiation that was really a stream of these particles. Irène Joliot-Curie [“ee-REN zhoh-LYOH kyoo-REE”] and Frédéric Joliot then saw that radiation knock protons out of paraffin wax, but they mistook it for gamma rays.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these neutral particles in atomic nuclei, discovered by James Chadwick in 1932.

tossups.p: In 1920, Ernest Rutherford predicted that atomic nuclei held a neutral particle about as heavy as a proton. Twelve years later, a scientist working under him at the Cavendish Laboratory in Cambridge proved that these particles exist.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these particles discovered by James Chadwick, which have no electric charge.

tossups.p: Outside an atom’s nucleus, one of these particles lasts only about 15 minutes on average before the weak force makes it decay into a proton, an electron, and an antineutrino. That process is called beta decay.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these neutral particles that sit alongside protons in the nucleus.

tossups.p: Physicists who trap these particles in a “bottle” and physicists who count their decays in a “beam” get average lifetimes that disagree by about nine seconds, a long-standing puzzle. That lifetime matters for working out how much helium formed after the Big Bang.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these neutral particles found in atomic nuclei, discovered in 1932.

tossups.p: In 1933, while waiting to cross a street in London, Leo Szilard [“SIL-ard”] imagined a chain reaction in which each atom that splits releases more of these particles. Szilard later patented that idea in Britain.
tossups.r: A uranium-235 nucleus that splits releases two or three of them. For 10 points, name these neutral particles that drive nuclear chain reactions.

tossups.p: Enrico Fermi found that these particles work far better at making elements radioactive after they are slowed down by passing through paraffin wax. Nuclear reactors use moderators such as graphite or heavy water to slow these particles down.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these neutral particles that, along with protons, make up atomic nuclei.

tossups.p: Boron’s isotope with mass number 10 is especially good at absorbing these particles. Control rods made of boron or cadmium soak up these particles to keep a nuclear reactor’s chain reaction from running out of control.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these uncharged particles found in the nucleus, which were discovered by James Chadwick.

tossups.p: Even though these particles have no electric charge, each one has a magnetic moment, a sign that it is built from smaller charged pieces. Those pieces are one up quark and two down quarks, whose charges add up to zero.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these particles found in atomic nuclei, about as heavy as protons but with no charge.

tossups.p: Clifford Shull and Bertram Brockhouse won the 1994 Nobel Prize in Physics for bouncing beams of these particles off solids and liquids to learn how their atoms are arranged and how they move. Because these particles have no charge, they slip deep into materials.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these neutral particles that share the nucleus with protons.

tossups.p: A few minutes after the Big Bang, about one of these particles remained for every seven protons, and nearly all of them ended up inside helium nuclei. Each helium-4 nucleus contains two of these particles.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these neutral particles that James Chadwick discovered in 1932, which sit in atomic nuclei.

tossups.p: The common isotope lead-208 holds a “magic” number of these particles, 126, along with a magic number of protons, 82, which makes its nucleus especially stable. Heavy stable nuclei like that one contain more of these particles than protons.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these particles whose number differs among isotopes of the same element.

tossups.p: The collapsed cores of some exploded stars, only about 20 kilometers across, are made mostly of these particles, which resist being squeezed together because of the Pauli exclusion principle. That resistance, called degeneracy pressure, keeps such cores from collapsing further.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these neutral particles that join protons in atomic nuclei.

tossups.p: Cosmic rays striking the upper atmosphere knock loose these particles, which turn nitrogen atoms into carbon-14 for radiocarbon dating. Carbon-14 has eight of these particles, two more than ordinary carbon-12.
tossups.r: An atom’s count of them equals its mass number minus its atomic number. For 10 points, name these neutral particles.

tossups.p: Ordinary hydrogen is the only stable kind of atom with none of these particles, while its isotope deuterium has one and radioactive tritium has two. Heavy water, made with deuterium, is used to slow these particles down in some nuclear reactors.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these neutral particles that, with protons, make up the nucleus.

tossups.p: In 1956, physicists at Berkeley’s Bevatron accelerator discovered the antiparticle of these particles. The scientist who first identified these particles won the 1935 Nobel Prize in Physics and later led Britain’s team on the Manhattan Project.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these uncharged particles, slightly heavier than protons, that James Chadwick discovered in 1932.

trap.title: Neutron, not neutrino
trap.body: The names sound alike because Wolfgang Pauli first called his ghostly particle a “neutron” before Enrico Fermi renamed it the neutrino, or “little neutral one,” after Chadwick found the much heavier neutron in 1932. Both have no electric charge, so “neutral” alone won’t tell you which one a tossup wants, and neutron stars are a separate answer line too.
trap.fix: The nucleus, isotopes, Chadwick, chain reactions, moderators, and control rods mean neutrons. Ghost particles, the Sun, oscillation, Super-Kamiokande, and IceCube mean neutrinos. A whole collapsed star about 20 kilometers across means neutron star.
trap.line: Real answer line: neutrons (prompt on nucleons, baryons, or hadrons; do not accept “neutrinos”)

topics.name: Torque
topics.kicker: The twisting effect of a force · Force times lever arm
topics.dates: Law of the lever described by Archimedes, 3rd century BCE
topics.briefing: Torque is the twisting effect of a force: it’s what turns a doorknob, a wrench, or a bicycle pedal. How much torque you get depends on how hard you push and how far from the pivot you push, which is why a long wrench loosens a stubborn bolt and why door handles sit far from the hinges. Torque is to spinning what force is to straight-line motion: it changes how fast things rotate.
topics.answerHtml: torque (accept moment of force; prompt on moment, tau, or twisting force; do not accept “angular momentum”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: This quantity’s name comes from a Latin word meaning “to twist.” This quantity is a vector that points along the axis of rotation, in a direction found with the right-hand rule, and it equals the cross product of the position vector from the pivot and the force.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this rotational equivalent of force, measured in newton-meters and symbolized by tau.

tossups.p: Archimedes [“ar-kih-MEE-deez”] stated a law of the lever that is really a rule about balancing this quantity, and he supposedly boasted, “Give me a place to stand, and I will move the Earth.” On a balanced seesaw, a heavier child must sit closer to the pivot so that both sides have equal amounts of this quantity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this twisting effect of a force, equal to the force times the lever arm.

tossups.p: In 1785, Charles-Augustin de Coulomb [“KOO-lohm”] measured electric forces with a torsion balance, using the fact that the amount of this quantity needed to twist a thin wire depends on the angle of the twist. Henry Cavendish later used a similar balance to measure the pull of gravity between lead balls.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this rotational effect of a force, symbolized by the Greek letter tau.

tossups.p: A loop of wire carrying an electric current in a magnetic field feels this quantity, which is what makes an electric motor spin. Earth’s magnetic field exerts this quantity on a compass needle, turning the needle until it points north.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this twisting effect of a force, measured in newton-meters.

tossups.p: A car engine’s power equals this quantity multiplied by how fast the crankshaft spins, which is why engine specs list both horsepower and this quantity, often in pound-feet. Low gears on a bicycle let a rider deliver more of this quantity to the rear wheel for the same push on the pedals.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this rotational equivalent of force, equal to force times lever arm and measured in newton-meters.

tossups.p: In the rotational version of Newton’s second law, the net amount of this quantity equals moment of inertia times angular acceleration. A wheel speeds up or slows down its spin only when a net amount of this quantity acts on it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this twisting effect of a force, symbolized by the Greek letter tau.

tossups.p: The net amount of this quantity on a system equals the rate at which its angular momentum changes, so angular momentum is conserved when this quantity is zero. On a tilted spinning top, gravity’s amount of this quantity makes the top precess instead of falling over.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this rotational effect of a force, measured in newton-meters and symbolized tau.

tossups.p: Alexander Calder’s hanging mobiles stay balanced because, at every pivot, this quantity from the pieces on one side balances this quantity from the pieces on the other side. An object is in static equilibrium only when both the net force and the net amount of this quantity on it are zero.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this twisting effect of a force, equal to force times lever arm.

tossups.p: A tall box tips over once its center of gravity moves past the edge of its base, because gravity then produces this quantity that turns the box over instead of back upright. Objects with wide bases and low centers of gravity are harder to tip over for the same reason.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this rotational effect of a force, symbolized by the Greek letter tau.

tossups.p: Mechanics use a special wrench that clicks when it reaches a set amount of this quantity, so that bolts such as a car’s lug nuts are tightened just right. That tool is named for this quantity.
tossups.r: A longer wrench gives more of it for the same push. For 10 points, name this twisting effect of a force.

tossups.p: Multiplying this quantity by the angle that an object turns through, measured in radians, gives the work done on the object. This quantity has the same units as energy, newton-meters, but those units are not called joules when they measure this quantity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this rotational equivalent of force, symbolized by the Greek letter tau.

tossups.p: Two equal and opposite forces that do not act along the same line, called a couple, produce this quantity without pushing an object in any direction. Turning a steering wheel with your hands on opposite sides creates such a couple.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this twisting effect of a force, measured in newton-meters.

tossups.p: Many cars with automatic transmissions use a fluid-filled “converter” named for this quantity to connect the engine to the wheels. Electric motors can deliver their greatest amount of this quantity even when they are barely turning, which helps electric cars speed up quickly from a stop.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this rotational effect of a force, equal to force times lever arm.

tossups.p: When you hold a weight in your hand, your biceps pulls on your forearm only a few centimeters from the elbow, so it must pull much harder than the weight to make enough of this quantity. In that case, the forearm acts as a third-class lever.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this twisting effect of a force, which is why door handles are placed far from the hinges.

tossups.p: Pushing straight toward a door’s hinges produces none of this quantity, because this quantity depends on the sine of the angle between the force and the lever arm. Its size equals the force times the perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of the force.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this rotational effect of a force, symbolized by the Greek letter tau.
