It times the angle turned (in radians) equals the work done
It shares units with energy (newton-meters), but those units are not called joules when they measure it
A couple: two equal, opposite forces not along the same line, like two hands turning a steering wheel
A fluid-filled “converter” named for it connects the engine to the wheels in many automatic transmissions
Electric motors give their greatest amount even when barely turning, so electric cars speed up quickly from a stop
The biceps pulls on the forearm a few centimeters from the elbow (a third-class lever), so it pulls much harder than the weight held
Low gears on a bicycle deliver more of it to the rear wheel for the same push on the pedals

trap.title: Torque or angular momentum?
trap.body: Torque, angular momentum, and moment of inertia all show up in the same spinning-object tossups. Torque is the twist that changes a spin, angular momentum is the amount of spin, and moment of inertia is how hard an object is to spin up. Saying just “moment” or “twisting force” earns only a prompt.
trap.fix: Wrenches, levers, seesaws, newton-meters, r × F, tau, and “force times lever arm” mean torque. Iω, spinning skaters, and Kepler’s equal areas mean angular momentum; mass spread far from the axis means moment of inertia.
trap.line: Real answer line: torque (accept moment of force; prompt on moment, tau, or twisting force; do not accept “angular momentum”)

topics.name: Power (physics)
topics.kicker: How fast work is done · Measured in watts
topics.dates: Horsepower defined by James Watt, late 1700s; the watt proposed in 1882
topics.briefing: Power is how fast work gets done or energy gets used: two people of the same weight who climb the same stairs do the same work, but the one who runs up uses more power. Power is measured in watts, named for steam-engine pioneer James Watt, who also came up with the horsepower so customers could compare his engines to horses. A 1,200-watt hair dryer uses 1,200 joules of energy every second.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: James Watt defined a unit of this quantity as 33,000 foot-pounds of work per minute, based on how hard he estimated a mill horse could work, so that buyers could compare his steam engines to the horses they replaced.
tossups.r: That unit, the horsepower, equals about 746 watts. For 10 points, name this rate at which work is done.

tossups.p: In an electric circuit, this quantity equals current times voltage, or current squared times resistance. A hair dryer that draws 10 amperes from a 120-volt outlet uses 1,200 units of this quantity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity measured in watts, the rate at which energy is used or transferred.

tossups.p: Electric companies send electricity over long distances at very high voltages, because for the same amount of this quantity a higher voltage means a smaller current, so less of this quantity is wasted heating the wires. Transformers raise and lower the voltage for that purpose.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, the rate of using or transferring energy, measured in watts.

tossups.p: For a car moving at a steady speed, this quantity equals the force pushing the car forward times the car’s velocity. For a spinning motor shaft, this quantity equals the torque times the angular velocity, so gears let a motor trade speed for twisting strength.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this rate at which work is done, measured in watts.

tossups.p: In a common school lab, students find their own value of this quantity by timing a run up a flight of stairs, then dividing their gain in potential energy, mass times g times height, by that time. Running up the stairs gives a larger value of this quantity than walking up them.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this rate of doing work, measured in watts or in horsepower.

tossups.p: A kilowatt-hour is not a unit of this quantity but a unit of energy, equal to using 1,000 units of this quantity for one hour. Electric bills charge for energy, while appliance labels list this quantity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, the rate at which energy is used, measured in watts.

tossups.p: A star’s luminosity is its total output of this quantity, which for the Sun is about 3.8 times 10 to the 26th joules every second. At the top of Earth’s atmosphere, sunlight delivers about 1,360 units of this quantity to each square meter, a value called the solar constant.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity measured in watts, the rate of energy transfer.

tossups.p: A resting adult’s body uses energy at a rate of roughly 100 joules per second, about the same as an old light bulb, and a trained cyclist can briefly produce more than ten times that much of this quantity.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this rate at which work is done or energy is used, measured in watts.

tossups.p: Dividing a machine’s useful output of this quantity by its input of this quantity gives its efficiency, which is always less than 100 percent because some energy turns into heat.
tossups.r: Doing the same job in half the time takes twice as much of it. For 10 points, name this rate of doing work.

tossups.p: The most extreme lasers reach enormous values of this quantity by squeezing a modest amount of energy into a pulse lasting less than a trillionth of a second. This quantity equals energy divided by time, so a shorter pulse with the same energy gives more of it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, measured in watts, that tells how fast energy is delivered.

tossups.p: The intensity of a sound or light wave equals the amount of this quantity it carries per unit area, and the decibel scale compares ratios of this quantity on a logarithmic scale. Doubling the amplitude of a wave multiplies the amount of this quantity it carries by four.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this rate of energy transfer, measured in watts and symbolized P.

tossups.p: James Prescott Joule found that the heat a current produces in a wire each second equals current squared times the wire’s resistance, which is the amount of this quantity turned into heat. That heating is how toasters and electric stoves work.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity, the rate at which electrical energy is used, measured in watts.

tossups.p: John Henry Poynting’s [“POYN-ting’s”] vector gives the direction and amount of this quantity flowing through each square meter of an electromagnetic wave. A solar panel’s rating gives the most of this quantity it can deliver in full sunlight.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity measured in watts, the rate at which energy is transferred.

tossups.p: An old incandescent bulb turns most of the electrical energy it uses into heat rather than light, so an LED bulb that gives the same amount of light needs only about a sixth as much of this quantity.
tossups.r: Bulbs are labeled with this quantity in watts. For 10 points, name this rate of energy use.

tossups.p: In 1882, William Siemens [“SEE-menz”] proposed naming a unit of this quantity for the Scottish engineer who improved the steam engine, and that unit later became part of the metric system. That unit equals one joule per second.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this quantity measured in watts, the rate at which work is done.

clues.t: The rate at which work is done or energy is transferred: work divided by time
Measured in watts; one watt is one joule per second
Its unit is named for James Watt, the Scottish engineer who improved the steam engine
Doing the same work in less time takes more of it, so running up stairs takes more than walking
Also measured in a unit named for horses, equal to about 746 watts
In a circuit, it equals current times voltage (P = IV), or current squared times resistance
A kilowatt-hour is a unit of energy, not of this: 1,000 watts used for one hour
For a moving object pushed by a force, it equals force times velocity
For a spinning shaft, it equals torque times angular velocity
Efficiency is useful output divided by input of it, always less than 100 percent
School lab: time a run up a flight of stairs, then divide mass times g times height by the time
Sent over long distances at high voltage, so a smaller current wastes less of it heating the wires; transformers change the voltage
Light bulbs are labeled in watts; an LED needs only about a sixth as much as an incandescent bulb for the same light
James Watt defined his horse-based unit as 33,000 foot-pounds of work per minute, to sell his steam engines
William Siemens proposed naming its unit for James Watt in 1882
A star’s luminosity is its total output of it; the Sun’s is about 3.8 × 10²⁶ watts
The solar constant: about 1,360 watts reach each square meter at the top of Earth’s atmosphere
A resting adult uses about 100 watts; a trained cyclist can briefly produce more than ten times that
The most extreme lasers reach huge values by squeezing modest energy into pulses shorter than a trillionth of a second
A wave’s intensity is the amount it carries per unit area; doubling the amplitude multiplies it by four
The decibel scale compares ratios of it on a logarithmic scale
James Prescott Joule: the heat a current makes in a wire each second equals current squared times resistance
The Poynting vector gives the amount flowing through each square meter of an electromagnetic wave
Germany’s PS (Pferdestärke, “horse strength”) is a metric horse-based unit of about 735 watts
China’s Three Gorges Dam can generate about 22,500 megawatts

trap.title: Power, not energy or work
trap.body: Power is how fast energy is used or work is done, so a kilowatt-hour on an electric bill measures energy, not power, and work and energy are separate answer lines whose tossups sound alike. The watt and the horsepower are units, not the quantity, and “electric power” used to mean electricity in general is not the physics idea of a rate.
trap.fix: Watts, horsepower, P = IV, “work divided by time,” or “how fast” means power. Joules, kilowatt-hours, and “force times distance” mean energy or work. If asked for “this quantity,” say “power,” not “watts.”
trap.line: Real answer line: power (prompt on P; do not accept “energy” or “work”)

topics.name: Liquids
topics.kicker: State of matter that flows · Fixed volume, but takes its container’s shape
topics.dates: Archimedes studied floating in them, c. 250 BCE
topics.briefing: A liquid keeps its volume but not its shape: pour a cup of juice into a bowl and it spreads out to fit, without getting any bigger or smaller. Its particles stay close together but slide past one another, which is why liquids flow, drip, and splash. Only two elements, mercury and bromine, are liquid at room temperature, and one of the slowest-flowing liquids ever studied, a lump of tar-like pitch, dripped only nine times from 1927 to 2014.
topics.answerHtml: Liquids (accept liquid state or liquid phase; prompt on fluids; do not accept “solid,” “gas,” or “plasma”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In 1927, Thomas Parnell set up an experiment to show his students that pitch, a tar-like substance that shatters under a hammer, is really this state of matter. Pitch in his funnel at the University of Queensland dripped only nine times between 1927 and 2014.
tossups.r: Substances in this state keep a fixed volume but take the shape of their container. For 10 points, name this state of matter between solid and gas.

tossups.p: Seismic S waves, which shake rock at right angles to their direction of travel, cannot pass through this state of matter, so they leave a huge “shadow zone” on the far side of Earth from an earthquake. That shadow zone showed that Earth’s outer core is in this state.
tossups.r: A solid turns into this state when it melts. For 10 points, name this state of matter.

tossups.p: Gallium, a metal used to make LEDs, changes into this state at about 30 degrees Celsius, so a piece of it held in a person’s hand soon becomes this state. Bromine, a reddish-brown halogen, is the only nonmetal element in this state at room temperature.
tossups.r: The only metal in this state at room temperature is mercury. For 10 points, name this state of matter, which flows and takes the shape of its container.

tossups.p: To read the volume of one of these substances, lab students look at the curved top surface, called a meniscus, at eye level in a graduated cylinder. Dropping a rock into a cylinder of one of these substances and seeing how far the level rises gives the rock’s volume.
tossups.r: Their volume is measured in liters and milliliters. For 10 points, name these substances, which have a definite volume but no definite shape.

tossups.p: Car brakes and hydraulic lifts work because these substances can barely be squeezed into a smaller volume, so a push on one end is passed through a sealed tube to the other. Blaise Pascal’s principle says that pressure applied to an enclosed fluid, like one of these, spreads equally throughout it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these substances, such as water or oil, that have a definite volume but no definite shape.

tossups.p: Once the vapor pressure of one of these substances matches the pressure of the air above it, bubbles of vapor form all through it, which happens to water below 100 degrees Celsius high in the mountains. Evaporation, by contrast, turns this state into a gas only at its surface.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this state of matter, which freezes into a solid and boils into a gas.

tossups.p: Oobleck, a mix of cornstarch and water named for a Dr. Seuss book, flows like this state of matter when poured slowly but turns firm when punched. Ketchup is one of these substances that gets runnier after it is shaken, an example of a non-Newtonian fluid.
tossups.r: Honey and syrup are thick examples of this state. For 10 points, name this state of matter, which has a definite volume but no definite shape.

tossups.p: Heike Kamerlingh Onnes [“KAH-mer-ling ON-us”] first turned helium into this state in 1908. Below about 2.2 kelvins, helium in this state becomes a superfluid that flows with no viscosity at all and can even creep up the walls of its container.
tossups.r: A gas condenses into this state when it cools. For 10 points, name this state of matter, which takes the shape of its container.

tossups.p: Above its critical point, a substance can no longer be separated into a gas and this state, so it becomes a supercritical fluid instead. At a substance’s triple point, its solid, its gas, and this state can all exist together, which happens for water at 0.01 degrees Celsius.
tossups.r: Ice turns into this state when it melts. For 10 points, name this state of matter between solid and gas.

tossups.p: In 1827, the botanist Robert Brown watched tiny particles from pollen grains jiggle randomly while floating in one of these substances. Albert Einstein later explained that jiggling as the result of countless molecules of the surrounding substance bumping into the particles.
tossups.r: Particles in this state are close together but can slide past one another. For 10 points, name this state of matter.

tossups.p: Two of these substances that will not mix, like the oil and vinegar in salad dressing, are called immiscible. A “density tower” stacks layers of honey, dish soap, water, and vegetable oil in one glass, with the densest layer at the bottom.
tossups.r: Water and rubbing alcohol are two of these that mix completely. For 10 points, name this state of matter that pours and takes the shape of its container.

tossups.p: A hydrometer, a weighted glass float, measures the density of one of these substances by how deep it sinks into it. Archimedes found that an object placed in one of these substances is pushed upward by a force equal to the weight of the amount it pushes aside.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this state of matter, which, unlike a gas, keeps a fixed volume.

tossups.p: In the Leidenfrost [“LYE-den-frost”] effect, a drop of one of these substances skitters across a very hot pan on a thin cushion of its own vapor. Sweat cools your skin because the fastest molecules escape from this state as vapor, carrying heat away with them.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this state of matter, which turns into a gas when it boils.

tossups.p: A paper towel soaks up one of these substances through capillary action, in which it climbs a narrow space on its own. Surface tension gives these substances a stretchy skin that lets water striders walk on ponds, and viscosity measures how slowly one of them flows.
tossups.r: Honey, milk, and water are examples of this state. For 10 points, name this state of matter.

tossups.p: The screens of many calculators and digital watches use special materials that flow like this state of matter while lining up their molecules like a crystal. In the kinetic theory of matter, particles in this state stay close together but have enough energy to slide past one another.
tossups.r: A substance enters this state at its melting point and leaves it at its boiling point. For 10 points, name this state of matter.

clues.t: Has a definite volume but no definite shape, so it takes the shape of its container
The state of matter between solid and gas: a solid melts into it, and it freezes back into a solid or boils into a gas
Its particles stay close together but slide past one another, which lets it flow
Water, milk, juice, oil, and honey are everyday examples
Mercury (a metal) and bromine (a nonmetal) are the only elements in this state at room temperature
Gallium, a metal used in LEDs, melts at about 30 °C, so it melts in your hand
Measured in liters and milliliters; read its curved top surface, the meniscus, at eye level in a graduated cylinder
Water displacement: a rock dropped into a graduated cylinder raises the level by the rock’s volume
Boils when its vapor pressure equals the air pressure above it (so water boils below 100 °C on mountains); evaporation happens only at the surface, at any temperature
Has surface tension (a stretchy skin that holds up water striders), viscosity (resistance to flowing), and capillary action (climbing narrow spaces)
Hardly squeezable, so car brakes and hydraulic lifts use it to pass a push along; Pascal’s principle says pressure spreads equally through an enclosed fluid
Two that won’t mix, like oil and vinegar, are immiscible; two that mix completely, like water and rubbing alcohol, are miscible
Archimedes: an object in it is pushed up by a force equal to the weight of the amount it pushes aside
Thomas Parnell’s pitch drop experiment (1927, University of Queensland): pitch shatters under a hammer, yet it dripped nine times by 2014
Seismic S waves can’t pass through it, leaving a shadow zone that showed Earth’s outer core is made of it
Heike Kamerlingh Onnes first turned helium into this state in 1908
Below about 2.2 K, helium in this state becomes a superfluid that flows with no viscosity and creeps up container walls
Above the critical point it can’t be told apart from a gas (a supercritical fluid); at the triple point it coexists with solid and gas (water: 0.01 °C)
Robert Brown (1827) saw tiny particles from pollen grains jiggle while floating in one; Einstein explained it as molecules bumping them
Oobleck (cornstarch and water, named for a Dr. Seuss book) flows when poured slowly but turns firm when punched
Ketchup is a non-Newtonian example that gets runnier after it is shaken
Leidenfrost effect: a drop skitters across a very hot pan on a cushion of its own vapor; sweat cools you as its fastest molecules escape
A hydrometer, a weighted glass float, measures its density by how deep it sinks
A density tower stacks honey, dish soap, water, and vegetable oil in one glass, densest at the bottom
Calculator and digital-watch screens use materials that flow like it but line up their molecules like a crystal (LCDs)

trap.title: Liquid, not fluid
trap.body: Fluids include both liquids and gases, since both can flow, so “fluid” only earns a prompt. Players also blurt out “water” when the question asks for the state of matter, or confuse liquids with plasma, the glowing fourth state. Liquid crystals, superfluids, and supercritical fluids are related ideas with their own names.
trap.fix: A definite volume but no fixed shape, melting, boiling, a meniscus, mercury and bromine, or S waves blocked by Earth’s outer core all mean liquid. If the substance fills its whole container, it is a gas; if it keeps its own shape, it is a solid. If the question says “this state of matter,” name the state, not an example like water.
trap.line: Real answer line: Liquids (accept liquid state or liquid phase; prompt on fluids)
